articles.title: Third-Line and Later Therapy for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis with Contextual Overview on Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Based Strategies in MSS/pMMR Disease.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple third-line and beyond (3L+) treatments for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) are available, yet no direct comparative evidence exists across all active regimens. TAS-102 ± bevacizumab, regorafenib, and fruquintinib have each demonstrated an overall survival benefit (OS). Recently, the first positive randomized data for an immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-containing regimen in an unselected microsatellite-stable/proficient mismatch repair (MSS/pMMR) mCRC population were reported (STELLAR-303). OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and safety of third-line and later-line therapies for MSS/pMMR mCRC using a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized trials, and to provide a contextual overview of ICI-based strategies. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a PROSPERO-registered systematic review and fixed-effects NMA of randomized trials in the 3L+ mCRC setting. Hazard ratios (HRs) for OS were extracted or derived from published reports and harmonized to a placebo/best-supportive care (PBO/BSC) reference using Bucher-anchored indirect comparisons. RESULTS: Thirteen trials formed a PBO/BSC-anchored, star-shaped OS network. Based on frequentist P-scores, TAS-102 plus bevacizumab ranked highest (0.99), followed by zanzalintinib plus atezolizumab (0.85), fruquintinib (0.68), and TAS-102 monotherapy (0.58). Regorafenib and other active regimens showed intermediate rankings, whereas atezolizumab monotherapy, nintedanib, and anlotinib ranked lowest. Pairwise relative treatment effects were generally consistent with the overall ranking pattern, although confidence intervals (CIs) overlapped for several treatment comparisons. CONCLUSION: TAS-102 plus bevacizumab was associated with the most favorable OS ranking, while zanzalintinib plus atezolizumab may represent a promising option. These findings support evidence-based sequencing of 3L+ therapies in mCRC and highlight the evolving role of multi-axis targeted and immune-modulatory strategies.

articles.title: Gut Microbial PncA as a Potential Target to Elevate NAD⁺ Biosynthetic Flux for Delaying Aging.
articles.abstract: Dysregulation of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) metabolic homeostasis is a key driver of aging. Because NAD⁺ biosynthetic flux directly reflects the actual rate of NAD⁺ production in cells and tissues, enhancing NAD⁺ biosynthetic flux plays a positive role in restoring its metabolic homeostasis and delaying aging. NAD⁺ biosynthesis comprises three major routes: the de novo synthesis pathway, the salvage pathway, and the Preiss-Handler (P-H) pathway. Supplementing biosynthetic precursors through these three pathways is an effective strategy to elevate NAD⁺ biosynthetic flux; however, its efficacy is constrained by the capacity of host tissues to convert and utilize specific precursors. Recent studies have demonstrated that the gut microbiota can deamidate nicotinamide (NAM) into nicotinic acid (NA) via nicotinamidase (PncA), channeling it into the Preiss-Handler pathway for utilization mediated by nicotinic acid phosphoribosyltransferase (NAPRT). In tissues where NAMPT-mediated salvage is compromised but NA utilization capacity remains intact, this conversion provides an alternative route for NAM recycling, thereby sustaining NAD⁺ biosynthetic flux. Within this gut microbiota-mediated deamidation bypass, the core enzyme PncA represents a potential target for delaying aging. Accordingly, this review focuses on the microbe-host NAD⁺ biosynthetic axis centered on gut microbial PncA as the key converting enzyme. After outlining the relationship between NAD⁺ metabolism and aging alongside current NAD⁺-boosting strategies, we systematically summarize the enzymatic mechanism, activity regulation, and gut microbial distribution of PncA; delineate the intestinal absorption and transport of NA and the tissue specificity of subsequent NAD⁺ biosynthesis; and discuss the remodeling of NAD⁺ metabolism mediated by precursor interconversion in light of host effects of microbe-derived NA and PncA intervention studies. By integrating microbial conversion with host utilization, we evaluate the interventional value of PncA as a potential pharmacological target for modulating biosynthetic flux and highlight its translational prospects in delaying aging and treating age-related diseases.

articles.title: Spatial Immunometabolic Context of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Ovarian Cancer: Evidence, Hypotheses, and Pharmacological Considerations.
articles.abstract: Ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), is characterized by marked spatial heterogeneity and limited benefit from immune-checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy. Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) are organized lymphoid niches associated with immune-active tumor states, but their biological and clinical implications depend on maturation, anatomical site, cellular composition, and treatment context. This review evaluates how spatial metabolic conditions may be associated with TLS organization and B-cell function in ovarian cancer. To prevent overinterpretation, the evidence is classified into four levels: direct evidence from ovarian-cancer TLS, indirect evidence from ovarian-cancer immune or metabolic studies, evidence from other tumors or lymphoid systems, and author-generated hypotheses requiring validation. We distinguish TLS morphology from germinal-center activity, somatic hypermutation (SHM), class-switch recombination (CSR), B-cell receptor (BCR) clonality, antibody affinity, antigen specificity, and effector function. We further discuss the context-dependent roles of lactate transport and hypoxia, including evidence that physiological germinal-center hypoxia and MCT1-dependent pyruvate metabolism can support selected B-cell functions. Spatial metabolomics and imaging mass cytometry may help test these relationships, but they do not by themselves establish causality or therapeutic predictiveness. Accordingly, pharmacological strategies are presented as mechanistically relevant candidates rather than validated TLS-directed treatments.

articles.title: Inhaled Nanomedicines for Pulmonary Fibrosis: Linking Pulmonary Barriers to Formulation Design and Translational Evaluation.
articles.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and disruption of alveolar architecture, leading to impaired lung function. Pirfenidone and nintedanib can slow lung function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, but do not reverse established fibrosis, and adverse effects may limit continued treatment. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities to improve pulmonary drug exposure through coordinated formulation and device design. This review briefly outlines pathological features relevant to delivery and examines how fibrosis modifies aerosol access, mucus transport, macrophage interactions and interstitial penetration. It distinguishes aerosol aerodynamic size from nanocarrier size and discusses design trade-offs involving surface charge, hydrophilicity and carrier mechanics in relation to target cells and disease context. Platforms are organized into polymeric systems, lipid-based systems, naturally derived extracellular vesicles, protein- and nucleic-acid-based assemblies, drug-based dispersions and powders, and carbon-based and coordination-framework systems. Nano-in-micro formulations are considered separately as an architecture connecting aerosol deposition with subsequent nanocarrier release. Selected micrometer-scale formulations provide comparative context for aerosol design. Representative studies are evaluated for delivery performance, therapeutic outcomes, safety and biodistribution, alongside advances in RNA delivery and combination strategies. Recent clinical developments in inhaled PF therapies are discussed separately from evidence for nanocarrier-based formulations. Evidence for most nanomedicine platforms remains preclinical. Further translation requires quantitative regional exposure measurements, functional delivery to intended cells, disease-relevant models, reproducible formulation-device performance and repeated-dose pulmonary safety.

articles.title: Plant-derived extracellular vesicle-like nanoparticles in ulcerative colitis: Current progress, mechanisms, and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with rising global incidence and substantial unmet therapeutic needs. Plant-derived extracellular vesicle-like nanoparticles (PELNs) have recently attracted growing attention as a potentially biocompatible and orally applicable therapeutic platform for intestinal inflammation. PURPOSE: This review aims to critically evaluate the current evidence regarding the biological characteristics of PELNs, their reported therapeutic effects in UC, the major mechanistic hypotheses proposed to explain their activity, and the key barriers that currently limit their clinical translation. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted using PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase, integrating keywords related to plant-derived extracellular vesicles and ulcerative colitis/inflammatory bowel disease ((plant-derived extracellular vesicles) OR (plant exosomes) OR (plant exosome-like nanoparticles) OR (plant nanovesicles) OR (Plant-derived extracellular vesicle-like nanoparticles) AND (ulcerative colitis OR inflammatory bowel disease OR colitis OR intestinal inflammation)). Reference lists of eligible articles were screened, and only peer-reviewed English publications were included. RESULTS: Available evidence suggests that PELNs may alleviate experimental colitis through multiple putative mechanisms, including modulation of intestinal inflammation, epithelial barrier protection, regulation of oxidative stress, and interactions with the gut microbiota. However, the field remains limited by unresolved issues in definition and nomenclature, lack of standardized isolation and characterization protocols, absence of validated positive and negative markers, and heavy reliance on reductionist preclinical models. In addition, mechanistic claims, especially those involving microbiota-mediated effects and cross-kingdom RNA regulation, are often supported by associative rather than causal evidence. Important translational questions related to biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, manufacturing scalability, batch reproducibility, long-term safety, and regulatory classification also remain insufficiently addressed. CONCLUSION: PELNs represent a promising but still immature therapeutic concept for UC. Future progress will require consensus terminology, source-adapted standardization of isolation and quality control, integrated multi-omics analyses linked to functional validation, and more rigorous translational studies to determine whether these plant-derived nanoparticle preparations can be developed into clinically credible interventions.

articles.title: Germline pharmacogenomics of platinum, radiotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity in non-small cell lung cancer: a mechanism-based systematic review and appraisal against CPIC evidence standards.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Germline variants predicting treatment toxicity guide care for a few drug-gene pairs, yet most reported associations never reach the clinic. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) isolates the problem: somatic genotyping is standard and toxicity limits dose intensity across chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy, yet no germline marker guides therapy. METHODS: Per a registered protocol (PROSPERO CRD420261364865), we searched four databases for 2020-2026 publications, synthesizing 35 studies from 15 countries. Thirty-four variant-toxicity associations were grouped by mechanism (transport/metabolism, DNA repair, immune regulation, target pathway). The 11 priority loci (12 variants) were benchmarked against the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) hierarchy. RESULTS: Twenty-nine of 34 associations were nominally significant. Of 10 studies correcting for multiplicity, seven had a finding that passed its own threshold (the lead association in five). Of 12 studies with validation analyses, three mounted an independent attempt (two with stated reservations), all nominally positive (single SNP, FDR-adjusted p=0.179; polygenic score; 27 patients); none replicated an association passing a multiplicity threshold. Across 23 significant lead associations, effect magnitude decreased with sample size (Spearman ρ=-0.48, 95% CI -0.81 to -0.07), consistent with selection-driven inflation. XRCC1 rs25487 effects differed by treatment and endpoint. No priority locus reached CPIC level A or B for its NSCLC drug pair. CONCLUSIONS: Many germline toxicity biomarkers are reported in NSCLC, but evidence remains exploratory: validation is uncommon, effect-size inflation is plausible, and within the review window no candidate met implementation standards. The bottleneck is evidence maturation, not discovery. We propose a four-phase framework toward genotype-guided care.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Natural Product Pharmacology: From Molecular Discovery to Precision Therapeutics.
articles.abstract: The use of natural products as a chemically diverse source of bioactive molecules for drug development has been well established; however, their multicomponent and multitarget nature, uncertain target causality, variable in vivo exposure, and heterogeneous responses to therapy make them challenging to characterize pharmacologically and translate into clinical practice. Systems pharmacology, together with artificial intelligence (AI), provides new approaches for molecular screening, target prioritization, integration of multidimensional data, and development of precision therapeutics. Osteoarthritis (OA), a heterogeneous whole-joint disease characterized by inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and tissue remodeling, serves as a representative model for evaluating such approaches. Network pharmacology can be used to organize relationships among natural product constituents, disease-related targets, and signaling pathways. AI can further assist with activity prediction, compound and target prioritization, multi-omics integration, and patient stratification. Studies combining network pharmacology, molecular docking, deep-learning-based affinity prediction, and experimental validation to narrow the list of potential candidate constituents and targets demonstrate the utility of computational methods in candidate prioritization. This article describes the transition of natural product pharmacology from empirical discovery and systems-based analysis to AI-enabled molecular discovery, mechanistic interpretation, pharmacokinetic assessment, and precision therapeutics. Although computational approaches may facilitate the identification and prioritization of biologically active constituents and targets, they remain limited by uncertainty regarding causality, inadequate in vivo exposure, model dependence, and insufficient clinical evidence. Future studies should focus on precise active-compound identification, direct target validation, systematic pharmacokinetic assessment, and high-quality clinical research to enhance the reliability and translational value of AI-enabled natural product pharmacology.

articles.title: Impact of intermittent hypoxia on drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters and drug pharmacokinetics: an underestimated concern in obstructive sleep apnea patients?
articles.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSA) is a prevalent and life-threatening respiratory disease. Marked by intermittent hypoxia (IH) and chronic inflammation, OSA frequently co-occurs with comorbidities like hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia or depression, necessitating various medications. However, the response to some treatments is notably compromised in OSA patients, manifesting as reduced efficacy and/or increased incidence of adverse events. The mechanisms underlying this altered pharmacological response remain unelucidated. Although comorbidities may substantially contribute to these alterations, IH and inflammation, key features of OSA, are known to modify drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters (DMETs). We therefore hypothesized that OSA/IH may affect DMETs, thereby altering drug pharmacokinetics and drug response. This narrative review synthesizes existing literature regarding the impact of OSA/IH on DMETs and pharmacokinetics both in experimental models and human, along with the underlying mechanisms exploring the roles of pro-inflammatory cytokines, transcription factors and epigenetics. Subsequently, we discuss the potential consequences of these IH-induced DMETs alterations on drug response in OSA patient population. In this purpose, we examine the hypothesis of pharmacokinetic modifications for each drug (or pharmacotherapeutic class) whose response appears altered in OSA patients. Additionally, we analyze the pharmacokinetic profile of the most commonly dispensed medications in OSA patients in order to identify additional drugs whose efficacy or safety might be compromised by IH-induced DMETs alterations. Finally, in the absence of conclusive clinical evidence, we propose priority research areas to better characterize the impact of OSA/IH on DMETs, pharmacokinetics, and drug response, and the underlying mechanisms.

articles.title: Serious Breaches in the European Union Under the Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014: A Systematic Analysis of Characteristics and Challenges.
articles.abstract: In the European Union, the reporting of serious breaches established by Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 represents major progress aimed at strengthening participant protection and ensuring data robustness throughout the EU. Namely, Article 52 of the Regulation introduces a mandatory reporting requirement for breaches likely to have a significant impact on participant safety or rights, or the trial data integrity. The reporting of serious breaches reinforces the sponsor's active responsibility for maintaining trial oversight and for timely communication with National Competent Authorities, aimed at ensuring adherence to regulatory requirements. This study provides the first systematic review of serious breaches notified under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using Italy as a case study to analyze the notification patterns, typologies, timelines, and seriousness assessments. Although the dataset is limited to serious breaches received by Italy and may not be fully representative of all serious breaches reported across the EU, it provides insights into the characteristics and distribution of serious breaches under the Regulation. It also aims to support stakeholders in consolidating harmonized approaches. In total, 320 serious breaches across 235 trials from 116 sponsors were analyzed; leading categories were investigational medicinal product administration/dosing errors (n = 73) and informed consent issues (n = 59). Inter-sponsor variability and reporting delays were observed, along with inconsistencies in the assessment of breach seriousness, suggesting opportunities for further harmonization of serious breach management. Continued monitoring of the serious breaches reporting process by the National Competent Authorities and inspection feedback should support harmonized and proportionate Regulation implementation across the European Union.

articles.title: Platelet-neutrophil immunothrombosis in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome and non-APS pregnancy morbidity during low-molecular-weight heparin-based prophylaxis.
articles.abstract: We prospectively studied 21 women receiving low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for APS or non-APS pregnancy morbidity and 21 healthy pregnant controls. Ten women were reassessed two years after LMWH discontinuation. Reference groups comprised 21 age-matched healthy non-pregnant women and five non-pregnant patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Blood was collected at 10-12, 20-22 and 30-34 weeks of gestation. Platelet and neutrophil activation, platelet-neutrophil aggregates and myeloperoxidase (MPO)-DNA complexes were quantified. Longitudinal biomarkers were analysed using participant-level mixed-effects models including study group, gestational stage and their interaction. LMWH effects were examined in vitro, and ex vivo NET generation was assessed in neutrophils from treated high-risk and untreated healthy pregnancies. Healthy pregnancy was associated with increased platelet P-selectin expression and MPO-DNA complexes, without broad neutrophil activation. Women reassessed off LMWH showed substantially higher platelet HMGB1, platelet-neutrophil aggregates, neutrophil tissue factor expression and MPO-DNA complexes than non-pregnant controls, with exploratory within-participant analyses supporting increases from pregnancy to postpartum. During LMWH treatment, most markers fell within the distributions observed in healthy pregnancy. Mixed-effects models provided no multiplicity-adjusted evidence of differences in gestational trajectories between healthy and treated pregnancies. In vitro, LMWH attenuated platelet activation and platelet-driven neutrophil responses, while neutrophils from LMWH-treated patients showed reduced ex vivo responsiveness. All index pregnancies resulted in live births. These findings indicate that platelet activation characterises healthy pregnancy. During LMWH treatment, most markers of platelet-neutrophil activation show distributions close to those observed in healthy pregnancy.Top of Form.

articles.title: Perivascular-like CD105⁺CD90⁺ adipose stromal cells promote anergy-like CD4⁺ T-cell hyporesponsiveness.
articles.abstract: Adipose stromal cells can suppress T-cell responses, but the contribution of stromal heterogeneity to CD4⁺ T-cell restraint remains poorly defined. Here, we show that murine CD105⁺CD90⁺ adipose stromal cells (ASCs) with perivascular-like features more strongly restrain activated CD4⁺ T cells than CD105⁻CD90⁺ ASCs in ex vivo coculture. Within a murine subcutaneous adipose atlas, CD105⁺CD90⁺ ASCs showed the strongest predicted communication with conventional CD4⁺ T cells exhibiting an anergy-biased transcriptional state. In coculture, CD105⁺CD90⁺ ASCs reduced splenic CD4⁺ T-cell proliferation, activation, and cytokine expression while increasing anergy-associated transcripts, consistent with anergy-like hyporesponsiveness. Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling revealed subset-biased stromal responses and reduced proliferation-associated programs in cocultured CD4⁺ T cells. Human breast single-cell and single-nucleus analyses identified partial transcriptional correlates of the murine CD105⁺CD90⁺ ASC (ASC_P) program in fibroblasts and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). In an exploratory ER-positive tumor cohort, the fraction of CAFs exhibiting a partial ASC_P-like transcriptional program correlated with conventional CD4⁺ T-cell anergy scores. In Luminal B breast cancer, higher ASC_P program scores were associated with higher CD4⁺ T-cell anergy-associated scores, Treg enrichment, and adverse outcomes. These findings identify perivascular-like CD105⁺CD90⁺ ASCs as a functionally specialized adipose stromal subset with an enhanced capacity to promote anergy-like CD4⁺ T-cell hyporesponsiveness.

articles.title: Identification of melanin synthesis inhibitors in Litchi chinensis pericarp procyanidins and the proposed mechanism.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hyperpigmentation disorders present significant therapeutic challenges. Although Litchi chinensis Sonn pericarp procyanidins (LPPC) show skin-lightening potential, the specific active constituents remain unclear. PURPOSE: To characterize the chemical composition of LPPC and investigate its anti-melanogenic activity and the tyrosinase-inhibitory mechanisms of its constituent procyanidins. METHODS: The major components of LPPC were structurally characterized by chromatographic separation and NMR, and quantified by mass spectrometry. Anti-melanogenic capacity was evaluated in A375 melanoma cells by quantifying melanin content, intracellular tyrosinase activity, and the protein expression of tyrosinase and tyrosinase-related proteins (TRP-1 and TRP-2). Primary bioactive procyanidins were identified through in vitro tyrosinase inhibitory screening. Molecular mechanisms were investigated using enzyme kinetics, fluorescence quenching, and docking simulations. RESULTS: LPPC effectively reduced melanin synthesis in A375 cells (IC50= 74.47 μg/ml) by suppressing intracellular tyrosinase activity and downregulating the protein expression of tyrosinase, TRP-1 and TRP-2 (with tyrosinase/TRP-1 reduced by approximately 60% at 100 μg/ml). Among seven identified compounds, epicatechin (15.3%) and procyanidin A2 (13.8%) predominated. Notably, A-type procyanidins A1 and A2 showed stronger tyrosinase inhibition than the tested B-type procyanidin and β-arbutin. Kinetic analysis identified procyanidins A1 and A2 as competitive inhibitors (Ki = 9.66 and 59.74 μM, respectively), which bind to key residues within the copper-binding catalytic center primarily through hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding. CONCLUSION: LPPC suppresses melanogenesis by downregulating melanogenic proteins and reducing intracellular tyrosinase activity, while LPPC-derived A-type procyanidins directly inhibit tyrosinsae in vitro. This study clarifies previously undefined aspects of the tyrosinase-inhibitory mechanism of LPPC-derived A-type procyanidins, including their competitive inhibition mode and active-site binding interactions with tyrosinase.

articles.title: Atractylodin remodels microglial lipid metabolism through deoxycholic acid signaling to suppress neuronal ferroptosis and alleviate depression-like behaviors.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic stress can disrupt hippocampal neuroimmune and metabolic homeostasis, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Atractylodin is a naturally occurring bioactive compound with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and metabolic regulatory activities. Its potential to ameliorate chronic stress-associated neuroimmune and metabolic disturbances warrants investigation, but its mechanisms of action remain unclear. PURPOSE: To determine whether atractylodin (ATR) alleviates chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced depression-like behaviors by restoring deoxycholic acid (DCA) signaling and microglial lipid homeostasis. STUDY DESIGN: A multilevel study integrated CUMS mice, hippocampal multi-omics, public human major depressive disorder single-nucleus RNA sequencing, microglia-neuron conditioned-medium experiments, and in vivo rescue and blockade interventions. METHODS: Behavioral, histological, and molecular analyses evaluated ATR efficacy. DCA was prioritized through untargeted metabolomics and targeted bile acid profiling. Mechanistic studies combined BV2 transcriptomics and lipidomics with inhibition of G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5/GPBAR1), stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) knockdown, oleic acid rescue, and conditioned-medium transfer to HT22 cells. Antibiotic treatment, DCA supplementation, and TGR5 inhibition were used for in vivo validation. RESULTS: ATR improved depression-like behaviors and hippocampal injury while restoring serum and hippocampal DCA. DCA remodeled the BV2 lipidome through TGR5-SCD1 signaling, restored unsaturated lipid signatures, and reduced lipid accumulation and pathological activation. TGR5 inhibition or SCD1 knockdown weakened these effects, whereas oleic acid partially rescued the SCD1-deficient phenotype. Conditioned medium from DCA-treated BV2 cells attenuated lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial injury, and ferroptosis-associated changes in HT22 cells. In vivo, antibiotics weakened ATR-mediated protection, DCA supplementation partially restored it, and TGR5 inhibition attenuated this protection. CONCLUSION: ATR restores DCA-dependent TGR5-SCD1 signaling to remodel microglial lipid metabolism, thereby suppressing microglia-mediated neuronal ferroptosis and alleviating depression-like behaviors.

articles.title: A review on gedunin as an anticancer agent: molecular mechanisms, preclinical evidence, and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gedunin is a limonoid natural product that has demonstrated anticancer activity in preclinical experimental models. However, findings vary across cancer types and experimental systems, and the extent to which its proposed molecular targets have been validated remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review evaluated the preclinical anticancer effects of gedunin, focusing on its reported molecular targets and signaling pathways, effects on cancer stem-cell phenotypes and chemoresistance, formulation and combination strategies, and translational limitations. METHODS: The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched from database inception to July 2026. Eligible studies were original, peer-reviewed investigations of chemically identified gedunin in in vitro, in vivo, or cancer-related mechanistic and biochemical models. Reviews, conference abstracts, preprints, studies of crude plant extracts without chemically identified gedunin, duplicate publications, and studies without relevant pharmacological or mechanistic outcomes were excluded. Data on cancer models, experimental conditions, gedunin concentrations or doses, molecular findings, pharmacological outcomes, and translational relevance were extracted. Because of differences in cancer models, experimental designs, and outcome measures, findings were synthesized narratively rather than quantitatively. RESULTS: The search identified 1048 records. Following removal of 877 duplicates, 171 records were screened by title and abstract, and 149 were excluded. Twenty-two full-text reports were assessed, of which four were excluded, leaving 18 independent original studies. Gedunin was reported to exert antiproliferative, pro-apoptotic, cell-cycle-modulating, anti-invasive, anti-stemness, and chemosensitizing effects across several experimental cancer models. Reported molecular associations involved heat shock protein 90 (HSP90)-related proteostasis, phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT), Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT), nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), Sonic Hedgehog/Glioma-associated oncogene (Shh/Gli), focal adhesion kinase/Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase (FAK/ROCK), oxidative-stress responses, and mitochondrial apoptotic signaling. Selected studies also reported activity against cancer stem-cell-associated phenotypes and drug-resistant models, while nanoformulation and combination approaches enhanced activity in experimental systems. Evidence for a direct interaction between gedunin and prostaglandin E synthase 3 (p23) was primarily derived from one study and remains insufficiently replicated. Overall, the evidence was dominated by in vitro investigations, with limited characterization of pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, systematic toxicity, and efficacy in clinically relevant in vivo models. CONCLUSION: Current evidence supports gedunin as a promising preclinical anticancer candidate, but not as a clinically validated anticancer agent or a compound with definitively validated molecular targets. The p23-HSP90 axis represents a candidate mechanism requiring independent confirmation through genetic perturbation, rescue experiments, direct target-engagement assays such as cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), and biophysical approaches including surface plasmon resonance (SPR) or isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). Future studies should prioritize standardized gedunin preparations, rigorous target validation, pharmacokinetic and biodistribution characterization, optimized delivery systems, systematic toxicological evaluation, biomarker-guided combination strategies, and validation in clinically relevant in vivo models. At present, safety evidence should be regarded as limited preclinical data; systematic toxicology remains unknown.

articles.title: Loureirin D alleviates ischemia-induced blood-brain barrier disruption via CD38-mediated suppression of microglial MAPK/JNK/ERK signaling.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a critical gatekeeper of central nervous system homeostasis, and its disruption represents a pivotal pathological mechanism underlying secondary brain injury and adverse clinical outcomes following ischemic stroke (IS). Consequently, therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving BBB integrity after ischemia hold substantial promise for IS treatment. Loureirin D, a bioactive flavonoid isolated from Dragon's blood, has demonstrated preliminary neuroprotective efficacy in photothrombotic stroke. However, whether BBB integrity is preserved in clinically relevant models of sustained, severe cerebral ischemia remains unknown, and the underlying molecular mechanisms remains to be elucidated. PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate whether Loureirin D protects against ischemia‑induced BBB disruption, and to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms. STUDY DESIGN: Combined in vivo and in vitro mechanistic studies using rat permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAO) model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD)‑exposed microglia‑endothelial co‑culture system. METHODS: A rat model of pMCAO was established by intraluminal filament insertion. Neurological deficits and BBB integrity were evaluated by Bederson scoring, Evans blue extravasation, brain water content, IgG leakage, and western blot of tight junction (TJ) proteins (zonula occludens-1[ZO‑1], occludin) and matrix metalloproteinase 2/9 (MMP2/9). An OGD model and microglia‑endothelial co‑culture were used to recapitulate the ischemic neuroinflammatory microenvironment, and the endothelial barrier function was assessed using transendothelial electrical resistance and dextran permeability. Transcriptomic profiling, molecular docking, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and small interfering RNA mediated knockdown were integrated to identify critical targets and mechanisms, with validation by western blot and immunofluorescence. RESULTS: Loureirin D markedly ameliorated neurological deficits and attenuated BBB disruption-as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation, brain edema, and IgG leakage-and suppressed the ischemia‑induced upregulation of MMP2/9 in pMCAO rats. Furthermore, it restored the expression levels of ZO‑1 and occludin. In OGD‑exposed bEnd.3 cells, Loureirin D directly attenuated apoptosis, downregulated Bax and Caspase‑3 proteins, and suppressed reactive oxygen species generation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis identified CD38 and Mapk11 as differentially expressed genes, and their dysregulation was subsequently validated at the mRNA level in ischemic brain tissues. Molecular docking simulations and CETSA, further supported by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay, collectively provided robust evidence for the direct physical interaction between Loureirin D and CD38. In OGD‑exposed BV2 microglial cells, Loureirin D suppressed microglial activation, as evidenced by reduced CD86 expression, and inhibited the phosphorylation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and p38, thereby attenuating MMP2/9 secretion. In a microglia-endothelial cell co‑culture system, Loureirin D preserved endothelial TJ integrity, as demonstrated by the sustained expression and proper localization of ZO-1 and occludin. These protective effects were abolished by CD38 knockdown, indicating a CD38-dependent mechanism. CONCLUSIONS: Loureirin D inhibits microglia activation by specifically targeting CD38, thereby suppressing the MAPK-MMP-2/9 signaling cascade and preserving BBB integrity. Concurrently, it directly protects brain microvascular endothelial cells against apoptosis and oxidative stress. Collectively, these findings establish a mechanistic rationale for the therapeutic potential of Loureirin D in IS and provide a translational foundation for the development of CD38-targeted interventions for neurovascular protection in cerebrovascular diseases.

articles.title: Integrating UHPLC-Q/TOF MS, network pharmacology and experimental validation to reveal the potential mechanisms and bioactive components of Zhuang medicine Longzuan Tongbi granules against rheumatoid arthritis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Longzuan Tongbi granules (LZTBG), a clinically validated eight-herb Zhuang medicine formula containing alkaloids, flavonoids, coumarins, and lignans, exerts anti-RA effects through multi-component, multi-target regulation. However, due to the complexity of its chemical composition, the anti-RA material basis and underlying mechanisms of LZTBG have not been systematically explored. PURPOSE: The objective of this study was to identify the active components and molecular mechanisms of LZTBG in the therapy of RA. METHODS: The chemical constituents of LZTBG were comprehensively characterized using UHPLC-Q/TOF MS coupled with feature-based molecular networking (FBMN). Serum pharmacochemistry was performed to identify absorbed components and investigate their in vivo metabolic patterns in rats. Network pharmacology combined with previously published metabolomics data was employed to predict core targets and potential regulatory pathways. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to validate target-ligand interactions. Finally, in vitro experiments using LPS-induced RAW264.7 macrophages were performed to verify the anti-RA effects and underlying mechanisms of the candidate compounds via ELISA, qRT-PCR, and Western blot analyses. RESULTS: A total of 235 chemical constituents were characterized in LZTBG, with alkaloids and coumarins identified as major active types. Serum pharmacochemistry detected 74 LZTBG-related compounds in rat plasma, revealing structure-dependent disparities in metabolic behaviors. Network pharmacology integrated with metabolomics highlighted ALOX5, MAPK3, and PIK3CA as core targets, with ALOX5 prioritized based on high-confidence protein-protein interaction evidence and topological significance. KEGG enrichment indicated primary involvement of lipid and atherosclerosis pathways. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that bergapten, magnoflorine, and marmesin bound stably to these targets, with MAPK and ALOX5 complexes displaying optimal structural stability. In vitro validation confirmed that these compounds significantly suppressed LPS-induced upregulation of IL-1β and TNF-α, downregulated ALOX5, MAPK3, and PIK3CA mRNA and protein expression, and inhibited ERK1/2 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner. CONCLUSION: This study systematically elucidates that bergapten, magnoflorine, and marmesin are the principal active components of LZTBG against RA. The therapeutic effects are mediated through multi-component, multi-target regulation of the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling pathways and their downstream inflammatory target ALOX5. The integration of multi-omics data with experimental validation provides a robust paradigm for deciphering the complex mechanisms of traditional medicines and highlights ALOX5 as a promising therapeutic target for RA intervention.

articles.title: Puerarin targets Piezo1 to restore autophagic flux for alleviating diabetic vascular calcification.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetic vascular calcification (VC), characterized by vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) osteogenic transition and extracellular matrix remodeling, is a major complication associated with increased cardiovascular mortality. Puerarin, an isoflavone compound derived from Pueraria lobata, exhibits vascular protective properties; however, its molecular targets and mechanisms against diabetic VC remain unclear. PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects of puerarin against diabetic VC and identify its potential molecular target and underlying mechanisms. METHODS: Primary VSMCs, MOVAS and HA-VSMCs cells were treated with high glucose and β-glycerophosphate (β-GP) to establish an in vitro calcification model. A streptozotocin (STZ) and vitamin D3 (VD3) were used to induce a mouse model of diabetic vascular calcification to evaluate the in vivo anti-calcification effects of puerarin. Transcriptomic analyses were utilized to identify the central dysregulated pathway and key molecular targets. Molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), fluorescence titration, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS) were performed to validate the interaction between puerarin and Piezo1. Calcium imaging, Piezo1 overexpression, knockdown and pharmacological activation of Piezo1 were further employed to verify the target of puerarin. RESULTS: Puerarin significantly attenuated vascular calcification in vitro and in vivo by inhibiting osteogenic differentiation and preserving the contractile phenotype of VSMCs. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that puerarin suppressed osteogenic transcriptional programs while restoring autophagy-related pathways. Mechanistically, puerarin directly bound to Piezo1 and inhibited Piezo1-mediated Ca²⁺ influx, leading to inhibition of AKT/mTOR signaling and restoration of autophagic flux. Overexpression of Piezo1 or pharmacological activation of Piezo1 with Yoda1 relieved the protective effects of puerarin on VSMC osteogenic differentiation. Notably, Piezo1 knockdown abolished the regulatory effects of puerarin on AKT/mTOR signaling and osteogenic differentiation, further demonstrating that the protective effects of puerarin are largely dependent on Piezo1. CONCLUSION: Our findings identify Piezo1 as a previously unrecognized direct target of puerarin and demonstrate that puerarin protects against diabetic vascular calcification by regulating Piezo1-mediated Ca²⁺ signaling and autophagy. This study provides new mechanistic insights into the vascular protective effects of puerarin and highlights its therapeutic potential for diabetic vascular complications.

articles.title: A new chylomicron-independent pathway is responsible for intestinal lymphatic transport of the S1PR1 immunomodulator SEW2871.
articles.abstract: It is well recognized that the intestinal lymphatic transport of lipophilic drugs is primarily associated with chylomicron (CM) formation and transportation, a process that can be promoted by co-administration of lipids. Here, we report that the sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) modulator SEW2871, an immunosuppressant that sequesters lymphocytes within lymphoid tissues, exhibits substantial lymphatic transport even in the absence of lipids, suggesting a CM-independent pathway. In thoracic lymph duct-cannulated rats, we compared the lymphatic transport of SEW2871 with the classic CM-dependent drug halofantrine following proximal small intestine (intraduodenal) administration. As expected, and consistent to documentations for typical lipophilic drugs in the literature, halofantrine showed high lymphatic transport with lipids (28.7%) but markedly lower (5.6-fold) transport without lipids (5.1%). In striking contrast, SEW2871 achieved very high lymphatic recovery (38.8% of the dose) in the absence of lipids. To further validate the CM-independent mechanism, we assessed SEW2871 absorption from the distal small intestine and subcutaneous tissue-sites incapable of endogenous CM formation. In both cases, SEW2871 maintained significant lymphatic recoveries of approximately 16% of the dose, whereas halofantrine transport was negligible under these conditions. Functionally, the enhanced lymphatic exposure after intraduodenal administration produced a markedly stronger inhibition of lymphocyte egress compared to the pharmacodynamic effect following intravenous infusion at the same dose, thereby demonstrating the therapeutic advantage of directly targeting the lymphatic system. Molecular docking revealed high binding affinity of SEW2871 to multiple macromolecules highly enriched in lymph, including albumin and apolipoprotein B isoforms, suggesting that SEW2871 may exploit alternative lymph-directing carriers to facilitate its uptake. Collectively, this study provides evidence for a new, CM-independent intestinal lymphatic transport pathway observed for SEW2871. Future elucidation of the exact mechanism may provide insights for developing next-generation lymph-targeted therapies.

articles.title: Vascular-targeted mild photothermal modulation of the blood-brain barrier enables efficient delivery of Pt(IV) prodrug to glioblastoma.
articles.abstract: Effective platinum chemotherapy for glioblastoma is constrained by the blood-brain barrier and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBB/BBTB), which limit intracranial drug exposure. Here, we developed PS@RGD-Pt nanoparticles that integrate a NIR photothermal semiconducting polymer, a reduction-responsive Pt(IV)-backbone polymer, and cRGD-functionalized PEG-PLGA to couple vascular targeting, mild photothermal barrier modulation, and intracellular platinum activation. In orthotopic GL261 gliomas, cRGD promoted nanoparticle localization at tumor-associated vessels. Irradiation by an 808 nm laser at 0.5 W/cm2 for 3 min raised the tumor-site temperature to 46.3 °C and transiently reorganized Claudin-5 and ZO-1. Extending irradiation to 6 min raised the temperature to 63 °C and induced glial activation, delineating a thermal-dose window. BBB/BBTB permeability peaked at 1 h and approached baseline within 24 h, without detectable alterations in vascular density, cerebral perfusion, neuronal or glial markers, memory, or locomotion. Within this mild photothermal window, intratumoral platinum accumulation increased by approximately 4.6-fold with low accumulation in the contralateral normal brain. Reduction-responsive activation of Pt(IV) enhanced tumor DNA damage and apoptosis. PS@RGD-Pt with irradiation prolonged median survival to 36 days, compared with 16 days for PBS, 20 days for nonirradiated PS@RGD-Pt, and 22 days for RGD-Pt with irradiation, while reducing systemic toxicity relative to cisplatin. These findings establish vascular-targeted, mild photothermal BBB modulation as a controllable strategy that couples reversible barrier opening with tumor-responsive platinum activation for glioblastoma treatment.

articles.title: Multi-omics and single-cell profiling characterize the protective effects of indole-3-acetic acid in hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is a major cause of liver dysfunction after hepatic surgery and transplantation. Sterile inflammation, myeloid-cell recruitment, and metabolic disturbance contribute to hepatic IRI, but effective immunometabolic interventions remain limited. Indole-3-acetic acid (3-IAA) is a natural plant auxin found in Arabidopsis thaliana shoot apices and young leaves and is also produced by microorganisms. Whether 3-IAA affects hepatic IRI is unknown. METHODS: We integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling to identify changes associated with hepatic IRI. We then evaluated 3-IAA pretreatment in a murine hepatic IRI model. Serum transaminases and histopathology were used to assess liver injury. CyTOF and single-cell RNA sequencing characterized immune-cell composition, functional signatures, and inferred intercellular communication. RESULTS: Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified 3-IAA among the metabolites showing lower hepatic abundance after IRI. 3-IAA pretreatment lowered alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase levels and reduced histological injury. CyTOF showed lower relative abundances of macrophages and neutrophils after 3-IAA treatment. Single-cell analysis identified fewer Ero1a+Bnip3+ macrophages and more C1qa+C1qb+ macrophages. These changes were accompanied by differences in maturation- and phagocytosis-related signatures. Neutrophil-associated transcriptional programs and inferred CCL, CXCL, MIF, TNF, complement, and galectin signaling also differed between groups. CONCLUSION: Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified lower hepatic 3-IAA abundance after IRI, and pretreatment with exogenous 3-IAA attenuated liver injury in mice. Protection was associated with changes in macrophage and neutrophil abundance, cell states, and inferred immune communication.

articles.title: Clinical translation of viral targeting of the endothelium in pulmonary vascular diseases.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary vascular diseases are characterized by endothelial dysfunction and progressive vascular remodeling. Most pulmonary vascular diseases, such as pulmonary hypertension, are rare but fatal. Although current therapies improve hemodynamics and clinical outcomes, they do not consistently restore endothelial homeostasis or reverse vascular remodeling, highlighting the potential of gene therapy as a disease-modifying strategy. AREAS COVERED: This narrative review examines the pulmonary vascular endothelium as a therapeutic target and discusses its heterogeneity, disease-dependent targetability, and its interactions with the other components of the vascular wall. We review adeno-associated viral, adenoviral, lentiviral and bocaviral vectors, including capsid/envelope engineering, receptor-mediated targeting, transcriptional and post-transcriptional restriction, and delivery routes. Therapeutic strategies such as gene replacement, transcription-factor delivery, and gene suppression are discussed, with particular emphasis on BMPR2. Translational barriers including viral vector immunity, species-dependent tropism, biodistribution, durability, controllability, manufacturing, and patient selection are also considered. EXPERT OPINION: Pulmonary endothelial gene therapy represents a highly promising but clinically immature approach. Progress will depend on vectors that achieve selective transduction of pulmonary endothelial cells while minimizing off-target accumulation. Improved preclinical models including large animals or human tissue may guide vector development. Novel targeted vectors will enable effective gene transfer, thereby reducing dose and vector-based immunotoxicity.

articles.title: Effects of efflux transporter genes on irinotecan-induced hematologic toxicity: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: AIM: Irinotecan is an anticancer drug used to treat colorectal and other solid tumours. Despite its efficacy, it has severe toxicities, including neutropenia and diarrhoea. The genetic association of UGT1A1 with irinotecan toxicity is reflected in Food and Drug Administration (FDA) drug labels; however, the effects of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter gene polymorphisms remain unclear. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the genetic effects of ABC transporters on irinotecan-related hematologic toxicity. METHODS: Relevant studies were searched on PubMed, SCOPUS and Web of Science. The meta-analyses were conducted using the Mantel-Haenszel method and the z-test. Heterogeneity was assessed using Higgins' I2 statistic. A random-effects model was employed to provide a more conservative effect. RESULTS: A total of 19 studies were included. Rs2032582 in ABCB1 was associated with a reduced risk of irinotecan-induced hematologic toxicity (OR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.25-0.91). Rs2292997 in ABCC5 and rs225440 in ABCG1 were related to increased risks of toxicity (OR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.23-3.43 and OR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.00-3.25, respectively). CONCLUSION: In conclusion, ABC transporter gene polymorphisms, particularly rs2032582 in ABCB1, may contribute to interindividual variability in hematologic toxicity of irinotecan. These findings may contribute to personalized therapy of irinotecan, after prospective validation.

articles.title: Implementation pathway of NAT2 genotype-guided isoniazid dosing in tuberculosis.
articles.abstract: N-Acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) is a major determinant of isoniazid exposure and contributes to clinically important variability in drug response during tuberculosis treatment. The poor-metabolizer phenotype is associated with increased isoniazid exposure and a higher risk of anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury, whereas the rapid-metabolizer phenotype is associated with reduced exposure and potentially unfavourable treatment outcomes. However, NAT2 genotype-guided dosing has not been widely implemented in routine care. In this narrative review, we summarize the biological, pharmacokinetic and clinical evidence for NAT2 and compare the translational pathways of TPMT-thiopurines, SLCO1B1-statins, CYP2C19-clopidogrel, DPYD-fluoropyrimidines and NAT2-hydralazine to identify considerations relevant to implementing NAT2-guided isoniazid dosing. These examples demonstrate that pharmacogenomic prescribing guidance and clinical implementation do not follow a single linear pathway and that initial prescribing recommendations have sometimes been developed without definitive randomized trial evidence. Importantly, the evidence needed to support prescribing guidance differs from that required to establish the clinical utility of routine testing. For NAT2, priorities include defining actionable phenotype-specific dosing and monitoring strategies; evaluating the complete test-to-treatment pathway; and generating further evidence on clinical effectiveness, feasibility and economic value across diverse settings. Carefully governed regional implementation with prospective evaluation, together with targeted comparative studies, may help strengthen the evidence base for future pharmacogenetic prescribing recommendations and the incorporation of NAT2 testing into clinical practice guidelines.

articles.title: Breaking barriers: advanced targeted drug delivery strategies for sensorineural hearing loss.
articles.abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is the most prevalent form of hearing impairment worldwide. However, drug delivery to the inner ear is severely hindered by the enclosed bony labyrinth and the highly selective blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB), resulting in suboptimal therapeutic outcomes and confining pharmacological management largely to symptomatic rather than etiological intervention. This review systematically dissects the multifaceted barriers to inner ear drug delivery and focuses on three core strategic pillars: (i) optimization of administration routes to balance invasiveness with cochlear bioavailability; (ii) rational selection of viral and non‑viral vectors guided by the unique pharmacokinetic properties of inner ear fluids; and (iii) functional modification of delivery systems with cell‑specific ligands to achieve precision targeting.Particular emphasis is placed on breakthrough advances such as LRP1‑mediated noninvasive trans-barrier delivery and prestin‑targeting peptide‑directed selective outer hair cell engagement. By integrating insights from drug delivery science, gene therapy, and targeted delivery research, this review proposes a conceptual framework to facilitate the clinical translation of precision medicine for SNHL. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from 189 peer-reviewed articles identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase databases (published between 1984 and 2026, focusing on advanced strategies to overcome the blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB).

articles.title: A scoping review of the role of pharmacogenomics in the discontinuation of psychotropic medication.
articles.abstract: The role of pharmacogenomics has been extensively investigated in relation to psychotropic treatment response and adverse outcomes. However, limited attention has been directed toward pharmacogenomic variability during discontinuation, which is frequently associated with withdrawal symptoms, relapse and other complications. Current deprescribing guidelines generally recommend gradual dose reduction but rarely account for genetic differences influencing discontinuation outcomes. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesize the current evidence regarding the role of pharmacogenomics in psychotropic medication discontinuation. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute's methodological framework, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science and PsycINFO were systematically searched for studies investigating pharmacogenomic factors related to the discontinuation of psychotropic medication (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, anxiolytics, hypnotics, stimulants and opioids). The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and findings were synthesized narratively. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria, comprising eight observational studies and five case reports. Included studies and case reports involved opioids (n = 8), benzodiazepines (n = 4), antidepressants (n = 4), antipsychotics (n = 1) and anxiolytics (n = 1), with four studies involving multiple medication classes. Gradual dose reduction was the predominant discontinuation approach; however, discontinuation protocols frequently lacked detail. Variants in CYP2D6, OPRM1, OPRD1, ARRB2, COMT, GNB3, GNAS, SLC6A4 and HTR1A were associated with discontinuation outcomes (withdrawal symptoms, adverse drug reactions and discontinuation syndrome). Pharmacogenomic variability may influence psychotropic medication discontinuation outcomes; however, current evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Larger prospective studies evaluating pharmacogenomic-informed deprescribing strategies are needed.

articles.title: β-hydroxybutyrate and cancer: an update on conflicting roles and therapeutic targeting.
articles.abstract: Cancer metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of malignancy, within which ketone body metabolism, particularly β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), has garnered significant attention due to its complex and paradoxical roles in tumor biology. This review systematically examines the multifaceted functions of BHB in cancer, spanning molecular mechanisms to clinical translation, and synthesizes the conflicting evidence regarding its tumor-suppressive and tumor-promoting effects. We first explore the potential of BHB as a diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive biomarker, where its differential abundance across cancers such as colorectal and pancreatic cancer underscores its context-dependent nature. We then examine the underlying molecular mechanisms that account for these opposing effects. A key focus of this review is the integration of recent advances in combination therapies involving BHB alongside chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and physical treatments, highlighting its emerging potential as a promising sensitizer for combination regimens. Finally, we systematically outline the core controversies and challenges in the field, attributing the diversity of BHB effects to heterogeneity in tumor metabolic phenotypes, molecular subtypes, and the tumor microenvironment. By constructing a framework that integrates mechanistic diversity, clinical evidence, and combination therapeutic strategies, this review underscores the imperative to shift from a "one-size-fits-all" paradigm toward precision stratification based on tumor metabolic phenotypes, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the development of safe and effective BHB/ketogenic diet-based combination therapies.

articles.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Ameliorates Ulcerative Colitis Through Multi-target Regulation of the NLRP3 Inflammasome: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), ulcerative colitis (UC)-like manifestations are commonly related to diarrhea, dysentery, chronic dysentery, and hematochezia. Classical prescriptions and medicinal materials used for these conditions are increasingly investigated for their capacity to regulate the NLRP3 inflammasome, a central inflammatory platform in UC. AIM OF THE STUDY: This review aims to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms of the NLRP3 inflammasome in the pathophysiology of UC and to systematically analyze the pharmacological mechanisms underlying TCM-mediated modulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome for UC amelioration. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, and MEDLINE were searched using the combined keywords "NLRP3 inflammasome," "traditional Chinese medicine," and "ulcerative colitis" and relevant intervention names. A systematic review was conducted on animal and cell studies that met the criteria. RESULTS: The available evidence indicates that TCM interventions can attenuate NLRP3 activation and downstream Caspase-1/GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis, enhance autophagy and mitophagy, regulate gut microbiota-derived metabolites, reduce mitochondrial oxidative stress, and influence upstream pathways including NF-κB, TLR4/MyD88, TXNIP, AMPK/ULK1, PINK1/Parkin, AhR, and Nrf2. However, most evidence is preclinical; clinical confirmation, standardized preparations, exposure-response data, and rigorous safety assessment remain limited. CONCLUSIONS: TCM provides an ethnopharmacologically grounded source of multi-component interventions targeting the NLRP3-centered inflammatory network in UC. Future studies should directly connect traditional indications with authenticated botanical sources, standardized chemical profiles, clinically relevant dosing, and well-designed randomized trials.

articles.title: Precision drug delivery for ulcerative colitis: engineering the colonic microenvironment for site-specific and responsive therapy.
articles.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterised by continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa, resulting from complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and dysregulated immune responses. Although conventional therapies, including aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics, and small-molecule drugs have improved disease control, their clinical utility remains limited by incomplete therapeutic responses, adverse effects, loss of efficacy, and difficulties in achieving sustained remission. The present review offers an in-depth view of the emerging trends in molecular pharmacology and future drug-delivery systems for UC. UC-relevant molecular targets and pathological features of the colonic microenvironment be matched to site-specific or stimulus-responsive delivery strategies to improve local therapeutic exposure while limiting systemic toxicity, and clinical translation have been described. We discuss recent therapeutic advances targeting key inflammatory pathways (e.g. TNF-α, JAK-STAT, TYK2, IL-23/Th17, S1P receptors and PPAR-γ) and microbiome-directed approaches (e.g. faecal microbiota transplantation, microbial metabolites and postbiotics). Biomarker-driven approaches, such as faecal calprotectin and microbiota profiling, are emphasised as key components of precision medicine and treatment monitoring. Advanced Drug delivery mechanisms such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles, hydrogels, microparticles, nanogels and multifunctional theranostic systems provide opportunities for colon-specific drug delivery, controlled release, improved bioavailability, improved mucosal targeting and decreased systemic exposure. New approaches based on RNA-based therapeutics, CRISPR/Cas technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted drug delivery system design further increase the possibilities of personalised treatment. To summarise, the combination of molecularly targeted pharmacology with intelligent and site-specific drug-delivery technologies is an exciting avenue for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and reducing treatment-related toxicity and for furthering personalised management of UC. However, translation to widespread clinical practice will need to overcome challenges related to biocompatibility, gastrointestinal variability, scalability, manufacturing, controlled release, and regulatory approval.

articles.title: Hydrogel-based drug delivery systems for the synergistic regulation of angiogenesis and osteogenesis.
articles.abstract: Bone defect repair remains a major challenge in clinical treatment, and insufficient vascularization is an important factor limiting bone regeneration. Owing to their favorable biocompatibility, extracellular matrix-mimicking three-dimensional network structures, and tunable degradation and drug release properties, hydrogels can encapsulate and locally release bioactive agents that promote angiogenesis and osteogenesis, providing a promising drug delivery platform for the coordinated regulation of angiogenesis and bone regeneration. This review comprehensively summarizes the applications of hydrogel-based drug delivery systems in the coordinated regulation of angiogenesis and osteogenesis during bone regeneration. First, we outline the biological mechanisms underlying angiogenesis-osteogenesis coupling. Second, we discuss passive controlled-release and active stimuli-responsive release strategies in hydrogels. Finally, we highlight the intrinsic relationships among the selection of therapeutic agents, drug release, and regenerative repair outcomes, while summarizing current challenges and future research directions. This review provides insights into the rational design of hydrogel-based therapeutic systems for vascularized bone regeneration and contributes to advancing research and development in this field.

articles.title: From prediction to functional delivery: evaluating artificial intelligence in lipid nanoparticle design.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the chemical and formulation space explored for nucleic acid lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), but accurate assay prediction does not by itself establish useful delivery in vivo. This critical narrative review examines how evidence links molecular design, complete formulation identity, and biological context to cell-resolved function, with a focus on mRNA. We distinguish tissue accumulation from functional cargo delivery, membrane damage from productive release, and target-cell coverage from panel-restricted on-target precision. Four purposively selected cases illustrate distinct inference problems: AGILE's selected-candidate association and reformulation, Hamilton's non-AI accumulation screen and functional follow-up, LANTERN's benchmark using AGILE-derived data, and Wang's delivery-classification and pKa-regression workflow with changes between screening rounds. We propose a claim-specific evidence audit and a prospective comparison whose primary outcome is the number of confirmed qualifying formulations found within a declared resource ceiling. Manufacturing, storage, and tolerability are considered where they constrain the application. Neither the audit nor the comparison design has been empirically validated. They identify testable requirements for evaluating whether AI improves a declared delivery decision.

articles.title: From direct inhibition to induced degradation: clinical progress of MCL-1-targeted interventions in cancer.
articles.abstract: MCL-1 is the most widely expressed and most rapidly turned over pro-survival member of the BCL-2 family, and the survival of acute myeloid leukemia, multiple myeloma, and many solid tumors depends at least in part on this protein. Several MCL-1-selective inhibitors have entered clinical trials; however, because cardiomyocytes also depend on MCL-1 for survival, direct inhibition has a structurally narrow therapeutic window, single-agent activity has been modest, and no inhibitor has been approved to date. In recent years, the research focus of MCL-1 targeting has shifted from direct occupancy toward downregulation and degradation. CDK9/BET transcriptional inhibition, translational and signaling interventions, pro-ubiquitination, and PROTACs and molecular glues lower MCL-1 within hours and reverse venetoclax resistance, although no degrader has yet entered a registered trial. At present, MCL-1 intervention is positioned mainly as a combination and sequencing component in resistant disease; response prediction relies on dynamic BH3 profiling, and cardiac safety monitoring is a common prerequisite across all routes. Looking forward, the first clinical validation of the degradation paradigm and biomarker-driven patient selection will determine the clinical prospects of this target.

articles.title: SENP3 loss in biliary tract cancer chemoresistance: substrate-specific control of fatty acid oxidation and mitophagy.
articles.abstract: Chemoresistance limits the benefit of first-line therapy in advanced biliary tract cancer (BTC); the mechanisms reviewed here were identified in models of acquired resistance to gemcitabine, a core component of combination regimens. Recent studies implicate loss of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO)-specific peptidase 3 (SENP3) in gemcitabine resistance through distinct upstream routes: METTL3-mediated N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification and YTHDF2-dependent decay of SENP3 mRNA in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC), and increased proteasomal degradation of SENP3 in gemcitabine-resistant gallbladder cancer (GBC) cells with reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS). In ICC models, SENP3 loss promotes stabilization of hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase trifunctional multienzyme complex subunit alpha (HADHA) through proposed SUMOylation-ubiquitination crosstalk involving K309 and K531, accompanied by enhanced fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and lipophagy-associated lipid mobilization. Trimetazidine attenuates the resistant phenotype in preclinical models, although HADHA-specific drug action has not been established. In GBC models, SENP3 loss increases SUMOylation of Reptin (RUVBL2) at K456, redirecting Reptin to the nucleus, where it upregulates PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and sustains a mitophagy-ROS feedback loop. CB-6644, an RUVBL1/2 ATPase inhibitor, enhances gemcitabine sensitivity and suppresses PINK1-associated mitophagy in GBC cells; the combination also showed antitumor activity in xenograft models, without establishing specific inhibition of Reptin K456 SUMOylation. This cross-substrate comparison reveals distinct protein-stability and subcellular-localization outcomes downstream of SENP3 loss and identifies substrate selectivity, potential FAO-mitophagy interactions, and clinical predictive utility as key questions for future investigation. Whether the two mechanisms coexist or interact within the same tumor remains untested.

articles.title: Targeting MicroRNAs in the perioperative window to prevent surgery-induced metastasis and postoperative cancer recurrence.
articles.abstract: Surgery remains a central curative treatment for many solid tumors; however, postoperative recurrence and distant metastasis continue to limit long-term survival. The perioperative period is increasingly recognised as a biologically active window during which surgical trauma, inflammation, wound repair, hypoxia, platelet activation, immunosuppression, anaesthetic exposure, and extracellular vesicle signalling may influence the survival and outgrowth of residual tumour cells, circulating tumour cells, and dormant micrometastases. MicroRNAs are particularly relevant in this context because they regulate coordinated gene networks involved in tumor survival, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, angiogenesis, immune escape, and metastatic niche formation. OncomiRs such as miR-21, miR-10b, miR-155, miR-210, and miR-221/222 may promote recurrence-associated signaling, whereas tumor-suppressive miRNAs including miR-34a, the miR-200 family, let-7, miR-126, miR-143/145, and miR-29 may restrict metastatic progression. This review provides a translational framework linking surgery-induced host responses with miRNA-mediated metastatic regulation. It discusses perioperative immune and stromal remodeling, anesthetic and analgesic influences, exosomal miRNAs, biomarker-guided monitoring, therapeutic delivery systems, safety concerns, and clinical trial design. Although perioperative miRNA therapy is not yet a validated clinical intervention, serial miRNA profiling combined with ctDNA, circulating tumor cells, cytokines, and clinicopathological variables may support future precision strategies to identify high-risk patients and guide recurrence-prevention studies. The key challenge is to suppress pro-metastatic signaling without impairing wound healing, infection control, or postoperative recovery.

articles.title: Global reporting of Brugada syndrome in VigiBase®: A disproportionality analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Brugada syndrome (BrS) represents a rare but potentially malignant cardiac channelopathy, which may be precipitated by drugs, although data mainly derive from case reports/series. OBJECTIVE: To describe the global reporting of BrS with drugs, including co-occurrence patterns, and identify novel potential associations. METHODS: We used VigiBase® to perform descriptive and disproportionality analyses. The reporting odds ratio (ROR) and Bayesian information component (IC) with relevant 95% confidence/credibility intervals (95% CI) were used as disproportionality measures to identify signals of disproportionate reporting (SDR). We performed a network analysis to assess the co-occurrence patterns of related medications based on Jaccard similarity. RESULTS: We included 544 deduplicated cases of BrS (94.7% serious events, 30.9% females, median time to onset of 30 days, 40.8% physician-reported, 63% from North America), with bupropion (n = 50), nortriptyline (n = 40) and flecainide (n = 34) as most frequently reported suspected drugs. Among 39 drugs with at least four reports, 32 emerged with an SDR, of which 17 were not listed in the BrS website (http://www.brugadadrugs.org), such as clozapine and loperamide (often overdosed). The co-occurrence network included 17 medications, regardless of the labelled role (suspected, interacting or concomitant), with a total of 12 potential co-occurrences; fentanyl exhibited the highest closeness centrality (1.0), whereas the strongest co-occurrence was reported between bupropion and nortriptyline (Jaccard similarity of 0.31). CONCLUSIONS: Notwithstanding limitations related to pharmacovigilance and the complex BrS pathophysiology, we identified 32 medications with over-reporting of BrS, including 17 drugs not listed in the BrS website as well as clusters in affective disorders and anaesthesia.

articles.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Glutamine contributes to ameliorate inflammation after renal ischemia/reperfusion injury in rats.
Berberine alleviates cobalt chloride-induced neurotoxicity in rats: associated changes in oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and inflammatory signaling markers.
articles.abstract: Cobalt chloride (CoCl2) induces neurotoxicity characterized by chemical hypoxia and oxidative damage, yet protective strategies remain limited. This study investigated the effects of berberine (BBR) against CoCl2-induced neurotoxicity in rats. Male Wistar rats (n = 7 per group) were treated daily for 14 days: control, BBR alone (100 mg/kg), CoCl2 alone (100 mg/kg), and CoCl2 with BBR (50 or 100 mg/kg). CoCl2 reduced central-zone time in the open field and increased latency to the target quadrant in the Morris water maze probe trial, whereas BBR produced only non-significant numerical improvements. CoCl2 disrupted redox homeostasis and altered hippocampal mRNA expression of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress markers, p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK), Janus kinase 3 (JAK3), signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 a (STAT5a), inflammatory mediators, and apoptosis- and autophagy-related genes. BBR improved antioxidant enzyme activities and was accompanied by attenuation of these changes, more strongly at 100 mg/kg. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) expression recovered at both doses, whereas reductions in heme oxygenase - 1 (HO-1), B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2), protein kinase B beta (AKT2), forkhead box O1 (FOXO1), c-Jun N-terminal kinase 1 (JNK1), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) were reversed only at 100 mg/kg. Immunohistochemistry indicated that BBR reduced glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and neurofilament light chain (NF-L) immunoreactivity and preserved brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Because gene expression was assessed at the mRNA level, findings are associative and require protein-level validation. BBR co-treatment was associated with reduced CoCl2-induced biochemical, molecular, and histological alterations, but no significant behavioral benefit.

articles.title: Integrative network toxicology, transcriptomic analysis, and experimental validation identify TOP2A-associated molecular alterations in NNK-related hepatocellular carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Accumulating evidence implicates nicotine-derived nitrosamine ketone (NNK) in the pathogenesis of various malignancies, yet the biological pathways underlying its effects on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have not been fully elucidated. To characterize the signaling pathways involved in NNK-driven hepatocellular carcinoma, we jointly applied network toxicology, single-cell RNA sequencing, molecular docking, virtual knockout analysis, and in vitro validation. Database mining identified 502 putative NNK-related targets across ChEMBL, CTD, SEA, and SwissTarget, together with 2143 HCC-associated genes retrieved from GeneCards, OMIM, and TTD. Functional enrichment analyses implicated the candidate genes in xenobiotic responses, cell cycle regulation, transcription factor binding, and several cancer-related signaling pathways, particularly the PI3K-Akt, FoxO, and p53 pathways. Following transcriptomic validation in GSE121248 and machine learning prioritization, TOP2A emerged as the leading candidate associated with NNK-related molecular alterations in HCC. TOP2A showed satisfactory discriminatory performance in both GSE121248 and GSE14520, with AUC values exceeding 0.75. Immune cell deconvolution further revealed associations between TOP2A expression and multiple immune cell subsets. In silico gene perturbation analysis identified ORM1 as a candidate gene associated with predicted TOP2A perturbation, suggesting a potential molecular relationship between TOP2A and ORM1 rather than an experimentally established regulatory axis. Subsequent cellular experiments showed that NNK treatment increased growth-related cellular activity and migratory phenotypes in both HuH-7 and Hep 3B2.1-7 cells. NNK exposure was also accompanied by increased TOP2A and ORM1 protein abundance, with consistent western blot findings observed in both HCC cell lines. In summary, this study identifies TOP2A as a potential molecular candidate associated with NNK-related HCC progression and suggests a possible relationship between TOP2A and ORM1 that may contribute to NNK-associated molecular alterations in HCC.
